1:
The word for bewitching sends the grammarians to the popular superstition. Robertson glosses baskaino as an old word kin to speaking, meaning to bring evil on a man by feigned praise or by the evil eye, found nowhere else in the New Testament, and notes that the papyri supply the adjective and adverb for unharmed by the evil eye and the noun for witchcraft; somebody, he says, some one aggressive Judaizer, man or woman, fascinated them. Chrysostom heads the superstition off where it stands in the gospel: the glance of the eye has no natural power to injure, the organ itself cannot be evil, and to behold is simply its function, while to behold in an evil manner belongs to a mind depraved within — the term stands for jealousy, which wealth and pomp generate because they are perceived by the eye. Ellicott takes the other reproach lexically, since foolish here is the word of the walk to Emmaus rather than the sharper word elsewhere: slow of heart names deadness of the moral affections, foolish the absence or undisciplined condition of the reasoning faculty, and the Gauls of Galatia were a people intellectually shallow and frivolous whom a little reflection would have kept from so gross an inconsistency.

Gill will not let the charge become a national one: it points neither to any Galatian reputation for rudeness nor to their old unregeneracy, which is common to all men and to God's elect before conversion, but to their present stupidity about justification, it being egregious folly to leave Christ for Moses and the Gospel for the law. Calvin hears passion rather than method, an expostulation inserted amid the doctrine because the rejection of the Son of God and the esteeming of his death as nothing would rouse any pious mind to indignation; the word he chooses means disordered in mind. Luther defends the disorder as design. Paul intermingles gentle exhortation with sharp reproof by his own rule to Timothy, to be instant in season and out of season, reprove, rebuke, exhort; the simple reader may think he keeps no order at all, and by the rhetoricians' measure he keeps none, but as concerning the spirit he observes a goodly order. Henry adds what makes the folly culpable rather than merely intellectual: it is not enough to know the truth and say we believe it, since we must obey it too, and those are spiritually bewitched who will not obey truth plainly set before them.

The argument that follows is a single question, and Barnes observes that the word only concedes as much: this was enough to settle the matter, and Paul did not need to go further than asking by what means they had obtained what they enjoyed. Wesley puts it as bluntly, that this one argument might convince them. Robertson finds the irony in the tenses of the next verse, a double contrast between having begun and finishing, the second a middle voice meaning finishing of yourselves. Clarke then dissents about what they had suffered, since the verb compounded with the adverbs for well or ill signifies to possess and enjoy as readily as to suffer loss; he would rather read it as asking whether they had received and lost so much good, the pardon of sins and the gifts of the Spirit, than as a reference to persecution. On the last verse the word for ministering draws out its own history: Ellicott explains that at Athens it was the technical term for a wealthy citizen bearing the cost of bringing out the chorus at the public feasts, so that it means liberal supply and not bare supply, while Clarke keeps the image closer, of leading up the chorus, adding grace to grace and benefit to benefit.
6:
Calvin marks the turn from experience to Scripture and defends the choice of witness: arguments drawn from examples are not always conclusive, but this one admits no exception in either the subject or the person, since there is no variety of roads to righteousness and in Abraham the universal rule for obtaining it has been laid down. Barnes and Clarke both press the chronology rather than the man. The most eminent of the patriarchs was justified before the law of Moses was given, so it cannot be pretended that the law is necessary to justification; and Clarke adds that the Jews themselves maintained as much, citing a rabbinic saying that Abraham could obtain an inheritance neither in this world nor in the world to come but by faith. Gill explains why the instance bites: Abraham was the first of the circumcision and the head of the nation, the very man the false teachers gloried in. Wesley says the same of his own day, that from Abraham the Jews still draw their great argument both for continuing in Judaism and for denying the Gentiles to be the church of God. Robertson notices that James quotes the same verse for obedience, and judges that the two apostles are discussing different episodes and both are right.

Robertson calls the inference astounding as addressed to Jews, that the real sons of Abraham are those whose sonship springs out of faith and not out of blood, and reaches for the precedents: John the Baptist calling descendants of Abraham a generation of vipers, and Jesus telling the Pharisees whose children they actually were. Whether Paul asserts this or commands them to recognise it is a genuine question, the Greek form serving for either; Calvin keeps the imperative as more energetic and argues from the scope that Paul is not presupposing the principle but exerting himself to convince them of it, and Ellicott, weighing the same ambiguity, comes down on the whole for the imperative as well. Ellicott then draws the consequence the argument was built for: faith, unlike the Law, is open to Gentile as much as to Jew, so a promise annexed to faith carried the death-blow of every exclusive privilege the Judaising party claimed and every burdensome regulation they wished to impose. Luther presses the point through a single word of the promise: lest the Jews should read nations of themselves alone, the Scripture forestalls them by saying not a father of nations but a father of many nations, so that neither law nor works nor carnal descent is in question.

The next verse personifies the Scripture, and the commentators handle the figure with care. Ellicott calls it a more decided personification than usual, the Scripture credited with foreseeing what God who inspired it foresaw, and notes that the metaphor falls in naturally because the Jews had a standing formula, What saw the Scripture, meaning simply what did it mean. Gill produces the formula itself, in that shape and in the parallel one about the law, and takes the personification to designate God as author. Robertson adds that the compound verb for preaching the gospel beforehand occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and that the quotation draws its all the nations from the later promise rather than the all the tribes of the earlier. Henry calls this preaching the gospel to Abraham, and infers that true believers of whatever nation are blessed with him and as he was. Calvin makes the preposition carry the weight: not with Abraham as circumcised, nor as a Hebrew, nor as one who might boast of works, but with the Abraham who by faith alone obtained the blessing, which here means adoption into the inheritance of eternal life. Luther says it by splitting the man in two, a working Abraham and a believing Abraham, and disclaiming all interest in the first.
10:
Robertson sees the curse hanging over the law-keeper like the blade over Damocles, and traces the word to its parts, a calling-down of imprecation; Paul quotes the close of the curses pronounced on Ebal, altering the Greek slightly so that it reads not of words but of things written in the book, which makes the idea plainer. Clarke turns the quotation into a textual case. No printed copy of the Hebrew Bible preserves the word answering to the apostle's all, and Jerome reports that the Jews suppressed it lest they should appear bound to perform everything written in the law; but the reading is not in doubt, standing in six manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi, in the Samaritan text, in several copies of the Targum, in the Septuagint, and in this quotation, where neither manuscripts nor versions vary. Gill is careful about who is threatened: Paul does not say those who were under the law, nor those who do its works, since the works of the law are to be done, only not for righteousness — it is the not doing that entails the curse. Wesley puts the impossibility plainly, that the law requires perfect, uninterrupted and perpetual obedience.

Calvin argues the next step from contradictories, since the same fountain does not yield both hot and cold: the law justifies the man who fulfils all its precepts, faith justifies those destitute of the merit of works who rely on Christ alone, and to be justified by one's own merit and by the grace of another are schemes that cannot stand together. He guards the point immediately, that the law is not contrary to faith in itself, or God would be unlike himself; the contradiction lies only in the matter of justification, where one may sooner unite fire and water. Ellicott reads the prophet's sentence with the stress on faith, and notes that just must be taken slightly ahead of itself, a man not being just before the exercise of faith but becoming so by it, the strict order running faith, justification, life. Robertson explains the phrase in the sight of God as meaning at God's side, as God looks at it, for the simple reason that no one but Jesus has ever kept his perfect law. On the following verse Clarke states the difference as a change of question, since the law asks not what a man believes but what he has done, and Wesley reduces it further: it does not say Believe, but Do.

The redemption verse draws the closest reading. Robertson completes the picture from the prepositions: we were under a curse, Christ became a curse over us, standing between us and what was overhanging, so that it fell on him and he bought us out. Barnes observes that the verb is not the usual one for ransom but the general word for purchasing, buying up, used here in only four places in all. Ellicott finds the force in the abrupt opening without a connecting particle, since the Law brought a curse and there stopped short, and the first thing the gospel does is undo that result. Calvin insists on the exact wording, that Paul does not say Christ was cursed but the stronger thing, that he was made a curse; he hung on the cross and so fell under it, and since he plainly did not suffer on his own account, either he was crucified in vain or our curse was laid on him. Luther spends his anger on Jerome and the schoolmen who, seeming to defend Christ from the reproach, said Paul did not speak in earnest and that Moses meant only a hanged malefactor. Clarke supplies why a hanged man was accursed and had to be buried the same day.
15:
Gill hears the address soften: having called them foolish Galatians, Paul now styles them brethren, hoping well of them still and imputing the blame rather to their teachers than to themselves. The illustration that follows is legal, and Clarke gives it in the forms of his own day, an agreement signed, sealed and witnessed, standing under the protection of the civil law so that nothing can be erased or added. Robertson supplies the vocabulary: the word serves for both covenant and will, the participle for ratifying is a perfect passive denoting completed and authoritative confirmation, and the verb for adding to it is found nowhere else — both parties may cancel a contract by agreement, but not otherwise. Calvin says the point is to put them to the blush, since it is base that the testimony of God should weigh less with us than a mortal man's; the argument runs from the less to the greater and leaves the immense distance between God and men still standing. Luther, remarkably, thinks the argument weak on its face and says so, holding that in weighty matters we ought to confirm earthly things by divine and not the reverse, which is the way of the schoolmen.

The argument from the singular noun is handled with varying degrees of comfort. Ellicott takes it straightforwardly, that the promise said seed and not seeds, descendant and not descendants, and that the Messiah is the descendant of Abraham above all others. Robertson is franker about the method, calling it a rabbinical refinement which is nevertheless intelligible, and pointing out that the word is a collective which Paul himself has just been applying to all believers, and that he does not claim Christ is specifically meant in the Genesis text. Clarke offers a reason the distinction is not arbitrary, since Abraham had two seeds in his house, one natural in his own household and one spiritual in those who were like him by faith. Calvin has no patience with the hesitancy, professing astonishment that Christians who saw the passage perversely tortured did not resist more determinedly but passed it slightly, as though it were undisputed ground. Luther renames the thing under discussion: the promise is a testament, and a testament is not a law but a donation, since heirs look for no burdens laid on them but for the inheritance confirmed. Henry marks the same difference, that the law promises to every man's person while the gospel promises first to Christ.

On the interval Robertson notes that the figure is the Exodus date for the sojourn in Egypt, and that the Greek version enlarges the wording to take in the patriarchs' years in Canaan as well. Ellicott strikes out two words of the received text here, since the oldest manuscripts omit the phrase that makes the covenant confirmed in Christ. Luther states the Jewish objection at full strength before answering it: God, mistrusting his own promises as insufficient to justify, added something better four hundred and thirty years later, so that the law abrogated the promise. Calvin blocks the narrower escape, that only ceremonies are in question; what Paul weighs is not the ceremonies themselves but the justifying effect attributed to them and the obligation laid on the conscience, and at the next verse he comprehends whatever interferes with a free promise. Ellicott states the incompatibility as a matter of terms, contract and free gift being incompatible ideas, and observes that the verb is a strong one, that God freely gave it. Wesley distinguishes the two arguments neatly, the first drawn from the time of the transaction and the second from its nature. Barnes recalls what the inheritance was, that Abraham should be heir of the world.
19:
If the promise settles everything, the obvious question is what the law was for, and Gill puts it in the objector's mouth: there had as good been no law at all. Ellicott answers from the word added, which makes the law no part of the original scheme but a sort of marginal addition, a parenthesis in the design of providence, the direct line running through the promise and its fulfilment while the law came in by the way. He notes that the phrase because of transgressions has been given two opposite senses, to check them or to multiply them, and thinks the expression wide enough to cover both. Robertson defends the consistency, since in Paul's mind the law is no part of the covenant but a thing apart which in no way modifies its provisions. Wesley divides the question by dividing the law: the ceremonial yoke was probably inflicted as punishment for the national sin of idolatry and was introduced only till Christ should come, while the moral law was added to discover and restrain transgression and does not pass away. Clarke keeps the figure of a straight edge laid against crooked conduct, given that we might know our sinfulness and our need of mercy.

Luther describes what the law does to a man rather than what it is for. When sin, death, wrath and judgment are revealed to him he cannot but grow impatient, murmur against God and despise his will, since he can neither bear the sentence nor escape it; the man who out of temptation was very holy, and bowed his knee and gave thanks like the Pharisee, now falls into hatred of God. Henry keeps the purpose in view instead, that the law was not designed to disannul the promise or set up a different way of justification. The verse about the mediator then stops everyone. Barnes reports Bloomfield's verdict that no passage in the New Testament has exercised so much learning to so little purpose, and that it seems to defy every attempt to elicit a satisfactory sense except by methods close to rewriting it; Ellicott counts two hundred and fifty or three hundred interpretations, by another estimate four hundred and thirty; Robertson simply says over four hundred have been made. Clarke, reviewing them, reports that Rosenmuller preferred Nosselt's, which makes Moses not the mediator of that one seed to whom the promise was given.

Calvin will not let the verse be made metaphysical: some philosophize that the twofold nature of Christ is not one in essence, but no man of sound judgment doubts that the contracting parties are meant, and the real question, left undetermined by the common exposition, is why the statement was introduced at all. He suggests it anticipates a wicked thought about a change in the divine purpose, as though God retracted his covenant the way men do. Wesley reaches the same end by a plainer route: there must be two parties or there is no mediator, God who made the free promise was only one of them, and Abraham was not present in the days of Moses, so Moses had nothing to do with the promise. On the closing verses the shutting up draws the images out. Robertson takes the verb as shutting together on all sides, like a shoal of fish in a net, or a lid closing over a chest that cannot be opened, or prisoners in a dungeon; Clarke has the Scripture lock men up until the sentence should be executed; Ellicott makes it a shepherd folding a flock so that it can stray neither right nor left.
23:
Gill guards the opening clause against a false inference. Faith coming does not mean the grace of faith was absent before, since the Old Testament saints had the same Spirit and the same faith as to its nature, object and use, and Adam, Abel, Enoch, Noah and Abraham believed in Christ and were justified by his righteousness as we are; what came was the doctrine of faith, preached earlier but never so clearly or so fully. Robertson reads the definite article the same way, as pointing back to the faith made possible by the historic coming of the Redeemer, and finds in the imperfect tense of the verb for guarding a long progressive imprisonment rather than a single act. Ellicott would render it kept in ward, the Law being a kind of prison-house and a stern guardian from whose custody escape was not permitted, and Clarke keeps the same picture of men held as in a strong hold and locked up. Calvin uses the temporal point to answer a question about the church rather than the individual: if Jew and Gentile make one church, the diversity of government is real but does not interrupt its union and harmony, the law having been given for a season.

The word rendered schoolmaster is agreed to be the wrong word, and the corpus spends its energy correcting it. Barnes explains that the office belonged to a slave or freedman to whose care boys were committed, whose main duty was not instruction at all but watching over them, restraining them from temptation and conducting them to the schools where instruction was given. Clarke says flatly that he is not the schoolmaster but the servant who led the children to school and brought them back and had charge of them out of school hours. Ellicott marks the boundary, that the pedagogue's care ceased where the schoolmaster's began, though it was he who chiefly formed the character, and recalls that Horace counted it a peculiar advantage that his own father had taken the place of pedagogue to him. Robertson fixes the years, from about six to sixteen, and completes the application: Christ is the schoolmaster, and the law as pedagogue kept watch until we came to him. Calvin reaches for the same distinction through the Greek terms, the conductor of children being one thing and the teacher another. Gill notices that the words to bring us are a supplement with nothing answering to them in the original.

Luther presses the comparison where it hurts. A schoolmaster is profitable and necessary, yet show me one scholar who loves his master; and what love the Jews bore Moses appears from their being ready at any hour to stone him, so it is not possible that the scholar should love the man set over him. Henry keeps to what the office could and could not do: the law taught no living, saving knowledge, but by its rites and above all its sacrifices it pointed to Christ, as children are led to school by the servants who have the care of them. Cyril of Jerusalem draws the same verse into an argument about the two Testaments, that the God of both is one, who foretold in the older the Christ who appeared in the newer, and who by the Law and the Prophets led us to Christ's school. Calvin dates the change by the veil of the temple rent in two, and concludes that under the reign of Christ there is no childhood left needing a schoolmaster, the law having resigned that office — though he at once puts the question again whether it is so abolished that we have nothing to do with it.
26:
Ellicott calls the English word children unfortunate here, because the whole point is that the Christian is no longer in the condition of a child but of a grown son: the age before the Messiah stands to the age after it as a minority stands to full age, and the believer has the standing of an adult son in his Father's house, released from pupilage. Calvin makes the same move from the other side, that it would not be enough to say we are no longer children unless it were added that we are freemen, since in a slave age alters nothing; being children of God is itself the proof of freedom. Robertson guards the phrase against a merely national sense, noting that Jesus could call the Jews sons of the kingdom in privilege though not in fact, and that God is Father of all men as Creator but spiritual Father only of those who receive adoption through faith. Gill lays out the three ways sonship might be meant and keeps only the third, neither by nature as Christ is nor by creation as Adam and the angels, but by adoption. Luther observes that Paul always has by faith, in faith, of faith in his mouth.

The clothing metaphor is worked over from several directions. Ellicott mentions the suggestion that it comes from the white baptismal robes, but prefers the ordinary usage of the Greek Old Testament, where the verb means to adopt or take to oneself. Robertson makes it a badge or uniform of service, like a soldier's, and adds that Paul is not saying a man is saved by means of baptism after the manner of the mystery religions. Barnes reads it of character, that they have put on his sentiments and opinions and characteristic traits as a man puts on clothes, which he notes was common language among ancient writers, and Clarke draws the obligation out of it: to put on a man is to assume his person and character, and whoever does so is bound to act his part. Luther divides the phrase in two, a putting on according to the law, which is to follow the example and virtues of Christ, his singular patience and inestimable mildness, and another according to the gospel. Calvin will have the union itself, that they are so closely joined to him as to bear his name and character before God and be viewed in him rather than in themselves. Henry keeps the profession in view.

On the abolished distinctions Robertson prefers there is not to there cannot be, a statement of fact rather than of possibility, and spells the fact out as the disappearance of race, of class and of sex rivalry, calling it a radical statement that marked out the path Christianity was to travel. Clarke thinks the third pair introduced with great reason, and documents the disparity it cancels from Jewish practice: a man might shave his head and rend his clothes in mourning where a woman was not permitted, and a man might impose the vow of the nazirite on his son where a woman could not on her daughter. Luther lengthens the list on his own account — neither magistrate nor subject, teacher nor hearer, master nor servant, mistress nor maid — and then guards it, since these are the good creatures of God and are nothing only in the matter of salvation. Ellicott notes that the pairs are meant to divide the human race exhaustively. Calvin closes by naming what the last verse is for: not to make descent from Abraham a higher thing than membership in Christ, but to repress the pride of those who reckoned no distinction higher than belonging to his race.
